Volume Two of Talleyrand's memoirs follows the French Empire at its height. Talleyrand, Napoleon's foreign minister for a decade, saw the great campaigns from inside. Beaufort's 1891 English version carries the story forward.

The narrative covers the years of victory, the making and breaking of alliances, and Talleyrand's slow split with Napoleon. His account of the road toward the Congress of Vienna begins here. He presents himself as the steady hand amid Napoleon's ambition. Historians read him with care, but his seat at the center makes the volume hard to skip. His portraits of Napoleon shift between respect and quiet resentment.
tamburlaine-the-great-part-2: Marlowe's sequel to his Scythian shepherd's conquests: Tamburlaine burns cities, defies gods, and is finally stopped only by death. "Infinite riches in a little room" gives way to cosmic defiance. Elizabethan drama at its most thunderous.
targums-etheridge-vol-2:
J. W. Etheridge published the second volume of his English Targums in 1865, finishing the Pentateuch begun in volume one. It covers Leviticus, Numbers, and Deuteronomy in the paraphrases of Onkelos and Jonathan ben Uzziel. These Aramaic versions were the people's Bible in the ancient synagogue.

Through the laws of sacrifice, the desert wanderings, and Moses' farewell speeches, the targums keep clarifying as they go. They explain hard commands, fill gaps in the story, and weave in teaching the rabbis prized. Etheridge's two volumes together made the whole Aramaic Torah open to English readers for the first time.
terence-comedies-sargeaunt-loeb-1912-vol:
Sargeaunt's second Loeb volume of Terence, published in 1912, holds Phormio, The Mother-in-Law, and The Brothers, with facing Latin text. Phormio, named for its quick-witted parasite, untangles two young men's love affairs against their fathers' plans. It is often counted Terence's most deftly built comedy.

The Mother-in-Law, which failed twice in Rome before it pleased, treats a young wife's secret with unusual delicacy. The Brothers debates two ways of raising sons, strict and easy, through two households. Terence's famous line that nothing human is alien to him sums up his manner. Sargeaunt's two volumes give the whole surviving Terence in the standard edition. His smooth Latin shaped European ideas of good style.
terence-comedies-sargeaunt-loeb-vol-2:
Terence, a former slave from North Africa, became Rome's most polished comic poet in the second century BCE. John Sargeaunt translated his plays for the Loeb series. This second volume holds the last three comedies: Phormio, Hecyra, and Adelphoe. With them, the six-play corpus of Terence is complete.

Phormio turns on a sly parasite who outwits two old men for a pair of young lovers. Hecyra, the Mother-in-Law, failed twice on stage before crowds took to its gentle plot. Adelphoe, the Brothers, weighs strict and soft ways of raising sons. Terence writes clean, humane Latin, and his lines were quoted in schools for two thousand years.
the-adventures-of-harry-richmond-volume-: Volume two of The Adventures of Harry Richmond is by George Meredith. Only a Project Gutenberg wrapper is present here. No novel text stands with it. The wrapper marks the part as number 51 in a Meredith set. It gives file 4445. It was first posted on January 31, 2002. It stands in edition 10 and plain ASCII. David Widger made the file.
the-adventures-of-tom-sawyer-part-2:
Part two of Mark Twain's The Adventures of Tom Sawyer opens at chapter four, on a calm Sunday in the village of St. Petersburg. The sun rises on a tranquil world, and breakfast gives way to family worship at Aunt Polly's house.

Her prayer is built, Twain says, from solid courses of Bible quotes with a thin mortar of her own words. She then reads a grim chapter of the law of Moses as if from Sinai. Tom must learn five verses for Sunday school and picks the shortest he can find, from the Sermon on the Mount. Sid has his lesson by heart days ahead. Readers get Tom's dread of church, a pinch beetle, and a poodle in the aisle.
the-amazing-marriage-volume-2:
Volume two of George Meredith's 1895 novel The Amazing Marriage holds Book Two, running from Small Causes to The Girl Madge. Its chapters track a bride from foreign parts given a taste of old England, a honeymoon in its first stage, and a trip down Whitechapel way.

Chapter Ten opens late at night with Gower Woodseer leaving Fleetwood and a band of late revelers at a hotel door. Under low stars he dwells on the lady's large grey eyes, rimmed dark and ringed with light. Meredith gives her a glamour no courtier can name, part beauty, part daring, part calm that holds men at a distance.
the-armourer-s-prentices-2:
Chapter One of Charlotte M. Yonge's novel of Tudor apprentices opens at the Verdurer's Lodge in the New Forest. A pair of lines from As You Like It stands at its head, about a poor portion left by a father's will, with which a young man means to buy his fortunes.

Forest officers, the chapter begins, have enjoyed some of the pleasantest dwellings in southern England since the days of the Conqueror. The Birkenholt home lies at the foot of a slope crowned with great beeches, their large silver boles rising like columns under a vault of tender green. Below the wood stretches pasture, flecked in season with lady-smocks, all silver white.
the-battle-of-the-strong-a-romance-of-tw:
Volume two of Gilbert Parker's romance opens at chapter ten with a ship named Narcissus entering rocky waters near the Ecrehos. Its first lieutenant, Philip d'Avranche, is rowed ashore by pilot Jean Touzel. Soundings and shore work have been ordered by the Admiralty.

Philip walks to a ruined chapel on Mattre Ile in a poor mood, bored by dull duty. He has been wrecked at Trinidad, served in America and India, and fought Spanish cruisers off Arabia. Now he waits for command of his own ship. His thoughts turn to Guida, a village beauty in Jersey, whose face he saw the day before.
the-bay-state-monthly-volume-3-no-2:
May 1885, volume three, number two, opens with a portrait of Sylvester Marsh and a life by Charles Carleton Coffin. Marsh is named as the projector of the Mount Washington Railroad. He was born on September 30, 1803, the ninth of eleven children, in Campton, New Hampshire.

Coffin describes settlers in the Pemigewasset Valley clearing pine, oak, and elm forest by hard labour before machines were common. Green fields replaced woods on the intervales and hillsides. He also tells of Arthur Scholfield, an English machinist who reached America three years before Marsh was born, forced to leave his tools behind under a British law.
the-boatswain-s-mate-captains-all-book-2:
W. W. Jacobs tells The Boatswain's Mate as part of his Captains All tales. George Benn, an old boatswain now out of the navy, has just asked Mrs. Waters, who keeps a small inn, to wed him. She turns him down with heat. She notes that he asks only after his third mug of ale, and he swears he will ask next time before he drinks a drop.

Benn walks off in gloom, his suit refused five times in two weeks. Two miles on he sits on a bank, lights his pipe, and dozes in the heat. He wakes at steps on the road and sees a tall, keen-eyed man with a pack, plainly an old soldier. The man stops, greets him in a warm way, and asks for a pipe of tobacco. Benn hands over his tin box and starts to chat.
the-boy-slaves-2: Capt. Mayne Reid wrote The Boy Slaves, and this copy is a new form of the book with a memoir by R. H. Stoddard. Thomas R. Knox and Company of 813 Broadway, New York, put it out as heirs to James Miller. A letter from Reid, dated New York, January 1, 1869, is also printed. In it he grants Fields, Osgood and Company the sole right to print his juvenile tales of adventure, called Boys' Novels, in the United States. No tale page is shown.
the-butterfly-s-ball-and-the-grasshopper:
The Butterfly's Ball and the Grasshopper's Feast is a verse tale for children. The heading names R. M. Ballantyne, and William Roscoe, with the date 1802. The verse starts with a call to the ball: come, take up your hats, and away let us haste. The trumpeter Gadfly has summoned his crew, and the revels wait only for the guests.

The ball is set on smooth-shaven grass beside the wood. Under a broad oak, old beyond memory, the children of earth gather with the tenants of air. They meet for an evening's amusement. The Beetle comes, blind and black, carrying the Emmet, his friend, on his back. The Gnat and the Dragonfly come, with all their relations, green, orange, and blue. They promise to lay by their sting for the evening. The Dormouse peeps out and leads his blind cousin the Mole to the feast.
the-castaway-odd-craft-part-2:
The Castaway, a tale from Odd Craft by W. W. Jacobs, opens in Shinglesea at the close of a short day, with Mrs. John Boxer standing at her shop door listening to the beat of the sea half a mile off. The little shop, with its wide-mouthed bottles of sweets, was her childhood home. Her husband was lost with the North Star three years before. Then she gave up her home in Poplar. She came back to help her mother.

Then the shop bell clangs, and she turns to a short, bearded man in the doorway, with oddly shaped shoulders and one leg not a match for the other. In a moment she is in his arms, sobbing and laughing together. The castaway has come home, and her mother, Mrs. Gimpson, wakes to share the uproar.
the-children-of-the-new-forest-2:
Captain Marryat's tale for young readers appears here in a second record, headed with the year 1847, and its opening matches the other edition of the same work word for word. The setting is England in 1647, after nearly five years of civil war. King Charles the First has been defeated and is held prisoner at Hampton Court.

With the Cavalier party dispersed and Cromwell's army gaining control of the Commons, Charles escapes in November. Sir John Berkely, Ashburnham, and Legg ride with him toward the Hampshire coast and the New Forest. A vessel for France was expected but never readied, so the king turns inland toward Titchfield, the Earl of Southampton's seat. Because the two records open with identical text, readers should treat this one as another edition of the same novel, not a sequel or a distinct story.
the-complete-poetical-works-of-percy-bys: Volume 2 of Percy Bysshe Shelley's complete poetical works is shown here in the Oxford Edition of 1914. Thomas Hutchinson edited that edition. Only the title page and the start of the contents are present. The list opens with early poems of 1814 and 1815. Among them stand Mutability, On Death, and A Summer Evening Churchyard. To Wordsworth also appears, with Feelings of a Republican on the Fall of Bonaparte. A note on the early poems by Mrs. Shelley is also listed. No poem text follows.
the-complete-writings-of-charles-dudley-: Volume 2 of Charles Dudley Warner's complete writings reached Project Gutenberg in June 2001 as etext number 2672. Nothing beyond the Gutenberg header is present: the usual copyright warnings, the note that the header must legally be seen first on opening the book, and the donation appeal.A title page and a contents list are all that stand here.
the-confession-of-a-child-of-the-century: Volume 2 of Alfred de Musset's Confession of a Child of the Century, in the French Immortals series, reached Project Gutenberg as etext 3940. Nothing but the header is present, with its April 2003 release date, its September 2001 first posting, and David Widger named as producer.Nothing inside the book follows its front matter.
the-confessions-of-harry-lorrequer-volum:
Volume 2 of Charles James Lever's Confessions of Harry Lorrequer covers chapters XI to XVII. It was printed at Dublin in 1839. Lever is named in brackets, since the title page names no author. The contents promise Cheltenham, Dublin boarding-house society, a chase, theatricals, a wager, and an elopement. A note flags a printer's slip: chapter XVI appears twice in the print copy.

Chapter XI opens on a cold, raw February evening in the coffee room of the Old Plough at Cheltenham. Harry sits alone, in the Latin tag's phrase, like Lucullus dining with Lucullus, with no companion. The chapter's business is a matrimonial adventure: showing how to make love for a friend. A Dublin chapter recalls Tom O'Flaherty and a reminiscence of the Peninsula. Lever keeps the tone of a mess-room story, where campaigns, matches, and practical jokes share the same breath.
the-diary-and-letters-of-madame-d-arblay: Volume 2 of The Diary and Letters of Madame d'Arblay (Frances Burney), with notes by W. C. Ward and Macaulay's essay as preface, covers 1787 to 1792. It was printed in London by Vizetelly and Company in 1891. An engraving shows George III, Queen Charlotte, and their family. The contents take up her court duties: the Queen's birthday drawing room, the equerries, the Duchess de Polignac, Mrs. Schwellenberg and her frogs, Mrs. Siddons, and Dr. Herschel. Only the title page and contents synopsis are present here.
the-divine-comedy-by-dante-illustrated-p:
Part two of Paradise in Dante's Vision, in the Rev. H. F. Cary's verse, opens at canto fifteen. True love falls silent so that Dante may pray, and a bright spirit runs down a cross of light like flame seen through pale stone. The shade greets Dante as his own blood and speaks of grace that let a living man enter heaven.

Here Dante meets a famed forebear who tells of old Florence and foretells his exile. War, faith, and family pride shape the talk. The sphere of Mars glows red with souls who died for the faith.

Cantos five through ten fill part two of Purgatory in Dante's Vision, in Cary's English verse. A spirit points at Dante, amazed that light breaks below his body, a sign he still lives. His guide rebukes his slow pace and tells him to stand firm as a tower that no blast can shake.

Souls who sang the Miserere draw near, stunned that a living man casts a shadow. Many here died by violence and turned to God at the last hour. Their tales plead for prayers from the living to speed their climb.
the-dore-bible-gallery-volume-2:
Volume two of The Doré Gallery of Bible Illustrations opens with the trial of Abraham's faith. The text retells Genesis in the old wording: God bids Abraham take Isaac to Moriah and offer him there. Abraham rises early, splits the wood, and walks three days to the place. Isaac asks where the lamb is, and his father says God will provide.

Doré's plate shows the altar scene in stark light and shade. Short Bible texts like this fill the volume, each set to face an engraving. Abraham's stayed hand is the volume's strong first note.
the-dwelling-place-of-light-volume-2:
Volume two of Winston Churchill's The Dwelling-Place of Light opens at chapter nine, with Janet Bumpus and her boss Ditmar. Their bond has tightened day by day, and Janet finds a keen, mixed joy in holding such a man on a leash that might snap. Alone, she falls into doubt, torn between new freedoms and old rules.

She fears she may match her wild sister Lise more than she thought. Desire, pride, and shame pull at her as the mill town heats up. Churchill keeps the lens close on a young woman's mind.
the-early-short-fiction-of-edith-wharton:
Volume two of The Early Short Fiction of Edith Wharton holds six tales with their first dates in magazines. Afterward dates to January 1910, The Fulness of Life to December 1893, Xingu to December 1911, and The Reckoning to August 1902. A verse list adds Botticelli's Madonna in the Louvre and The Tomb of Ilaria Giunigi, both from 1891.

Afterward opens with a joke in a bright June garden about a house's one ghost, whom its owners will never know. Mary Boyne recalls the jest in December dusk, and its bite lands. Wharton blends wit with quiet dread.
the-forsyte-saga-volume-2: This Penguin printing of The Forsyte Saga, Volume 2, holds The White Monkey, The Silver Spoon, and Swan Song, and the front matter here is a life of John Galsworthy. It tells of his birth in 1867, Harrow and Oxford, his call to the Bar in 1890, and his turn to writing under Joseph Conrad's sway and his wife's. It dates the three novels to 1924, 1926, and 1928, and notes his Nobel Prize of 1932. No page of the novels can be read here.
the-french-revolution-volume-2:
Hippolyte A. Taine wrote this second volume on the French Revolution as The Jacobin Conquest, part of his Origins of Contemporary France. Two books trace how a small, tight party took hold of a vast land.

The first book studies the Jacobins: their rise, their clubs, their press, and theircast of mind. The second shows the first stage of the conquest, with rigged votes, hunts for foes, and scare tactics. Taine then weighs the Legislative Assembly, its skill, its sessions, and its warring groups. His verdict is cold: a creed, held by few, ruled France by fear and club craft.
the-gaming-table-its-votaries-and-victim:
Andrew Steinmetz wrote The Gaming Table as a two-volume study of gambling in all times and lands, with stress on England and France. This first volume is given to the Duke of Wellington.

In his preface Steinmetz calls the book a set of facts and a slice of social history worth thought. Forty or fifty years before his day, he says, gambling was the rage in London. Squares now full of staid folk once held gaming rooms packed with votaries of chance. Dice, cards, and the turf bred sharpers, ruined lords, and odd codes of honor, and Steinmetz sets out to trace them all.

Andrew Steinmetz wrote this second volume of The Gaming Table on the folk who live by chance and the games they play. The contents run from polite sharpers to fortune telling by cards and amusing card tricks.

The first chapter traces the chevaliers d'industrie, smooth sharpers found in each city. To win trust they pair with men of good name. Or they forge titles of their own. Later heads take up pro game folk and their frauds. They take up duels and deaths among gamblers. They take up the great clubs and the math of chance. They end with the tales of dice and cards, from piquet to faro and hazard.
the-gilded-age-part-2:
Part 2 of The Gilded Age: A Tale of Today is dated 1873. Mark Twain and Charles Dudley Warner wrote the novel. This part opens with Chapter X. Days after a funeral, papers are found on the dead Major Lackland. Lackland once held a seat in Congress. He lost all trust after he sold his vote for cash.

The papers show a shock. Laura Hawkins was not the child of Mr. and Mrs. Hawkins. The papers name no real parents. Neighbors fill the gap with gossip. Each tale of her birth grows more dark and more wild. Laura soon meets cold looks and turned heads. Her place in the town starts to shift.
the-golden-bowl-volume-2: Henry James wrote The Golden Bowl. This record is Volume II of the novel. Only front matter is present here. It is a Project Gutenberg header. The header gives a long notice on copyright laws. It tells readers to keep the file as it is. It honors the volunteers who made the text. It gives the title and author, a release date of July 2003, and Edition 10. No page of the novel itself is present. Nothing about this volume's own chapters can be told from what is here.
the-great-conspiracy-volume-2:
John Logan wrote The Great Conspiracy: Its Origin and History. This record is Part 2. It opens with Chapter VI, The Great Conspiracy Maturing. The 6th of November, 1860, has come and passed. By the 7th, the conviction that Lincoln would be elected has become a certainty. The fact has been heralded across the Republic.

Logan describes the excitement. Republicans in the North rejoiced. The great wrong of slavery, they felt, was to be placed in the course of ultimate extinction. Douglas Democrats felt gloomy forebodings at their leader's defeat. Much of the Southern Democracy openly exulted. The long-wished-for chance for a revolt of the slave power was at hand. South Carolina rejoiced with bonfires and processions. Fire-eaters were jubilant in Charleston.
the-heart-of-mid-lothian-volume-2:
Walter Scott wrote The Heart of Mid-Lothian, Volume 2. The tale belongs to Tales of My Landlord, second series. The title page credits Jedediah Cleishbotham as collector and arranger. Chapter first opens with lines from Measure for Measure. Mrs. Saddletree then enters a room of hidden misery.

An old man lies in bed after a long swoon. The curtains are drawn around him. Jeanie sits motionless at his side. Mrs. Saddletree is kind but not delicate. She opens the window and draws the curtain back. She urges the old man to bear his sorrow well. Jeanie, pale as ashes, asks if all is over.
the-home-book-of-verse-volume-2:
Burton Egbert Stevenson edited The Home Book of Verse, Volume 2, by various poets. A note states that the contents of the set stand in Volume 1, while the pages present open Part II, Poems of Love. The first poem shown is Eros, by Ralph Waldo Emerson, dated 1803-1882, on how love is a short sense of the world that men and gods have not outlearned.

A second poem, Now What Is Love, follows in question form. Love is called a fountain and a well where pleasure and repentance dwell, a work on holiday, December matched with May, and sunshine mixed with rain. Love poems in many voices fill the part, set for home reading.
the-ink-stain-tache-d-encre-volume-2: Volume two of René Bazin's The Ink-Stain continues a three-part split. The pages present here hold only an old etext header. No chapter of the novel itself appears. The header gives the file as etext 3973. Release came in April 2003. The volume stands sixtieth in the French Immortals series. It stands second among Bazin's works there. Readers seeking the story's middle find only the wrapper. The header names the book, its author, and its place. Nothing more can be read from what is present.
the-land-of-midian-revisited-volume-2: Richard F. Burton published volume two of his Midian travel account in London in 1879, completing a two volume work. Only the title page and contents are present here, listing chapters eleven through nineteen on ruins at Shuwak and Shaghab, a turquoise mine, the Sharr mountain, southern marches, and gold mine ruins. The march narrative and the appendices on the three journeys do not appear in this record.
the-landlord-at-lion-s-head-volume-2:
William Dean Howells continues his summer hotel novel in part two, opening at chapter twenty-seven. Jackson Durgin has kept a promise to write to the painter Westover, and he writes home to his mother each week that winter. Snow cuts the branch trains, so mail comes by cutter from Lovewell.

Jombateeste, the French Canadian helper, teases Cynthia by pretending he dropped a letter on the road. The scene shows winter isolation at the hotel and the weight letters carry there. Family pride, love, and ambition press on the Durgin household through the cold months.
the-lane-that-had-no-turning-volume-2:
Gilbert Parker fills volume two of his Pontiac tales with four pieces, opening with the absurd romance of P tite Louison. Medallion the auctioneer knows her five brothers after selling them part of a farm. Illness later brings him into their home, where the brothers guard Louison with formal, constant courtesy.

Medallion senses a hidden romance behind their homage and their care with talk of marriage. Other pieces in the volume cover a little bell of honour, a son of the wilderness, and a worker in stone. Parker writes French Canadian village life with warmth and gentle mystery.
the-legends-of-the-jews-volume-2: Louis Ginzberg continues his gathering of Jewish legend in volume two, translated from his German manuscript by Henrietta Szold. Only the title page and contents are present here, covering Bible times from Joseph to the Exodus. Sections follow Joseph as favorite son, slave, prisoner, dream reader, and ruler of Egypt, then Jacob blessing of his sons and the tribes. The legends themselves, retold in full prose, are not included in this record beyond those headings.
the-letters-of-elizabeth-barrett-brownin: Frederic G. Kenyon edited Elizabeth Barrett Browning letters with biographical additions, and the third edition appeared in 1898. Only the title page and contents of volume one are present here, listing chapters from her birth and early poems through Hope End, Sidmouth, Torquay, and Wimpole Street. A final chapter here reaches the poems of 1844 and a proposed journey to Italy. The letters themselves do not appear here.

Frederic G. Kenyon edited Elizabeth Barrett Browning letters with biographical additions, and volume two of the third edition appeared in London in 1898. Only the title page and the start of the contents are present here. A chapter for 1851 and 1852 opens the list. Its topics include Casa Guidi Windows, Venice, Milan, Paris, and the coup d etat in France. The letters themselves, from her married life in Italy and beyond, remain outside this record.
the-letters-of-horace-walpole-earl-of-or: Horace Walpole letters fill four volumes, and volume two covers 1749 to 1759. Only the title page and a detailed contents list are present here, naming letters to Sir Horace Mann and George Montagu on Parliament debates, peace fireworks, masquerades, Methodism, and Garrick marriage. Newly collected letters are marked in the list with a special letter. The correspondence itself, with Walpole sharp gossip on London society, is not included in this record.
the-letters-of-robert-louis-stevenson-vo: Sidney Colvin selected and edited Robert Louis Stevenson letters to family and friends, and this record title page names volume two. Only the title page and contents are present here, listing life at Bournemouth, a second stay in the United States, winter in the Adirondacks, and Pacific voyages. One odd clash stands plainly: the file header above the title page repeats the volume one wording found in the volume one record. The letters themselves do not appear here.
the-life-and-adventures-of-baron-trenck-:
Thomas Holcroft translated Baron Trenck memoirs, and Cassell issued volume two in London in 1886, six years before the volume one edition held here. Its introduction differs from the companion volume: pages here trace Holcroft own life instead of the Trenck cousins. He wrote about thirty plays, four novels, and many translations.

Holcroft also faced a high treason charge in 1794 for sympathy with French revolutionary ideas, then won discharge without trial. The memoirs first appeared at Berlin in 1786 and 1787. Readers learn how a radical English playwright carried a Prussian adventurer story across languages.
the-life-and-letters-of-maria-edgeworth-:
Augustus J. C. Hare edited the life and letters of Maria Edgeworth, and volume two opens mid journey in her own words. Maria writes to Miss Waller from Coppet on September 1, 1820, describing Swiss travel from Berne toward Thun. Low carriages with tarpaulin awnings jolt the party along mountain roads.

She marvels at the Lauterbrunn valley, chestnuts and sycamores, and snow peaks above summer flowers. The Staubach waterfall looks like strings of water and faintly disappoints her. Clear air also tricks the party about distance to a Grindelwald glacier, turning a short stroll into a two mile walk.
the-life-of-charlotte-bronte-volume-2: Elizabeth Cleghorn Gaskell wrote the life of Charlotte Bronte, and this record holds volume two. Only a detailed contents summary is present here, tracing her father cataract operation, the writing of Jane Eyre, its reviews, the deaths of Branwell and Emily Bronte, and the start of Shirley. Anne Bronte last illness at Scarborough also fills a chapter summary. The biography itself, built from letters and Haworth visits, is missing from this record beyond those summaries.
the-life-of-joan-of-arc-vol-1-and-2:
Anatole France wrote his life of Joan of Arc, and Winifred Stephens translated it for John Lane in London and New York in 1909. A note to the English edition thanks scholars who praised his research rules. Named critics found errors that he fixed for this edition, and Andrew Lang scruples led to added references.

France says hagiographers alone attack him, not for error but for explaining Joan at all. They want her story left mysterious and supernatural, while he restores natural causes from strong sources. Volume one of two opens a rational, literary life of the Maid.
the-life-of-napoleon-i-volume-1-of-2: John Holland Rose wrote his life of Napoleon the First with new material from British official records, and this record holds volume one of the 1910 Bell edition. Only the title pages and the start of the contents are present here, opening with a note on the Republican calendar and a chapter on parentage and early years. The work was first published in 1901 and revised several times by 1910. The biography itself stays beyond the pages held in this record.
the-life-of-napoleon-i-volume-2-of-2: John Holland Rose wrote his life of Napoleon the First with new material from British official records, and this record holds volume two of the 1910 Bell edition. Only the title page and contents are present here, listing chapters from Ulm and Trafalgar through Austerlitz, the fall of Prussia, Tilsit, the Spanish rising, and the empire at its height. A Russian campaign chapter closes the list shown. The biography itself does not appear here.
the-life-of-the-rt-hon-sir-charles-w-dil: Stephen Gwynn began the life of Sir Charles W. Dilke, and Gertrude M. Tuckwell completed and edited it as his literary executrix. Only the title page and contents of volume two are present here. Chapters run from home affairs in 1883 through Egypt and franchise reform. The fall of Khartum and the start of the Home Rule split in 1886 follow in the list. The narrative and Dilke memoirs themselves cannot be seen in this record beyond those chapter titles.
the-literary-remains-of-samuel-taylor-co: Volume the Second of The Literary Remains of Samuel Taylor Coleridge was collected and edited by Henry Nelson Coleridge. The record holds only a title page and contents, leaving the pieces themselves unread. The contents open with extracts from Coleridge's letters, then turn to a large section on Shakespeare, with introductory matter on poetry, the drama, and the stage. Listed topics include a definition of poetry, Greek drama, Shakespeare's judgment and genius, and notes on plays from The Tempest and A Midsummer Night's Dream through Coriolanus.
the-love-affairs-of-great-musicians-volu: Volume II of Rupert Hughes's The Love Affairs of Great Musicians is dated 1903. Only the title page, contents, and list of illustrations are present here, so the chapters themselves do not appear. The contents list Franz Liszt, Richard Wagner, a chapter called Tschaikovski, the Woman-Dreader, The Heart of a Violinist, an omnibus chapter, and Robert Schumann and Clara Wieck, closing with Musicians as Lovers. Illustrations include Miss Smithson as frontispiece, George Sand, and Princess Carolyne von Sayn-Wittgenstein with her child.
the-magus-or-celestial-intelligencer-bei: Only a digitization leaf and a garbled title page are legibly present here, so the work itself does not appear. The leaf records digitization by the Internet Archive in 2016 with funding from the Wellcome Library. The title page, cleaner in a companion record that carries a Glasgow Ferguson Collection stamp, names The Magus, or Celestial Intelligencer, a complete system of occult philosophy in three books. It promises the cabalistic art, natural and celestial magic, and effects worked through celestial influences and the occult properties of metals, herbs, and stones.
the-marble-faun-or-the-romance-of-monte-: Nathaniel Hawthorne's The Marble Faun, or The Romance of Monte Beni, is split across two volumes, and this record is volume two. Only a contents list is present here, so the romance itself does not appear. Oddly, that list begins by listing volume one's chapters in full, from Miriam, Hilda, Kenyon, Donatello through The Faun's Transformation and Miriam and Hilda. Volume two's own chapters follow: The Tower among the Apennines, Sunshine, The Pedigree of Monte Beni, Myths, The Owl Tower, and On the Battlements.
the-mayflower-and-her-log-july-15-1620-m: Nothing of Azel Ames's history itself shows in this record; only its Project Gutenberg wrapper survives here. That wrapper identifies the title as The Mayflower and Her Log, volume 2, and lists a June 2003 release as etext 4102. David Widger produced the file, according to the credit line. Beyond the volume number, the wrapper offers the usual Gutenberg notes on public domain editions, donations, and the foundation's tax status, with no chapter text at all.
the-modern-regime-volume-2:
Hippolyte A. Taine's The Modern Regime, Volume 2, is volume 6 of The Origins of Contemporary France. Its contents cover Book Fifth, on the Church and its moral institutions, and Book Sixth, on public instruction, meaning state education, with a chapter following its evolution between 1814 and 1890.

Taine died in March 1893, and his nephew Andre Chevrillon prepared Taine's last manuscripts, dealing with the Church and education, for publication. Chevrillon's preface explains the plan: treat the Church, the school, and the family, and describe the modern setting in which French society works. Napoleon had organised France's moral and intellectual bodies, Chevrillon writes, and finishing that study would have brought Taine to view France as a whole.
the-money-master-volume-2:
Volume 2 of Gilbert Parker's The Money Master carries Epoch the Second, chapters IV to XII, and opens with Chapter IV in full. Thirteen years have passed. The parish weighs its new cure against Jean Jacques Barbille, now its leading man since the old cure, Pere Langon, died at eighty-five.

Jean Jacques had prospered in out-of-the-way country. His flour mill ground well, his saw-mill more than paid, and his farms showed a small profit. An ash-factory of his own starting lost only a little, and his lime-kilns earned money despite past mismanagement. He also lent money, dealt in horses, acted as fire insurance agent, and sold lightning rods. The new cure, M. Savry, is young and must earn the love the old priest commanded freely.
the-monkey-s-paw-the-lady-of-the-barge-a:
W. W. Jacobs's story collection The Lady of the Barge and Other Stories opens here with its best-known tale, The Monkey's Paw. The record is labelled Part 2 of the set. Outside, the night is cold and wet; inside Laburnam Villa, the parlour fire burns brightly behind drawn blinds.

Mr. White and his son Herbert play chess while Mrs. White knits by the fire. The father, fond of radical changes in the game, keeps landing his king in needless danger. Having spotted his own fatal mistake too late, he talks loudly about the wind and their slushy, far-out road to keep Herbert from noticing. Herbert calmly announces check, then mate. Heavy footsteps at the gate then announce the visitor the family half expected.
the-notebooks-of-leonardo-da-vinci-volum:
Volume 2 of Leonardo da Vinci's notebooks, in Jean Paul Richter's 1888 translation, opens with the notes on sculpture. Far fewer notes deal with sculpture than with painting, and they are scattered through the manuscripts. Richter places them first in this section, numbered from 706 onward.

Many of the notes concern the bronze horse for Francesco Sforza, a monument Leonardo worked on for years. Richter gives pride of place to notes on casting the statue, since they are the fullest and may help rebuild the lost work. Sketches of moulds, iron supports, and one galloping horse design add to the written record.
the-onlooker-volume-1-part-2: The Onlooker was a New York weekly magazine edited by Alfred Henry Lewis, sold for five cents, or one dollar a year. Volume I, part 2, is dated May 28, 1902. Only the cover pages and contents are present here, so the articles themselves do not appear. The contents name The Casual Club, with items on Tammany and its missing funds and Mr. Croker gone for good, plus a poetry section called As You Like It.
the-ordeal-of-richard-feverel-volume-2: Only the Project Gutenberg header is present here for volume 2 of George Meredith's novel The Ordeal of Richard Feverel. The header names the title and author. It gives the etext number 4407 and says the file was first posted on December 28, 2001. No title page or chapter text appears in what is present. The etext was produced by Pat Castevans and David Widger, and it is the thirteenth Meredith item in the Gutenberg series.
the-parent-s-assistant-or-stories-for-ch:
Maria Edgeworth's The Parent's Assistant, or Stories for Children, appears here in a 1903 Macmillan edition, with an introduction by Anne Thackeray Ritchie and illustrations by Chris Hammond. The title page notes the Hammond illustrations were first printed in 1897. Ritchie recalls being a little girl with inflamed eyes, unable to read, when her father read her the story of the Little Merchants from this book.

The tale lasted two mornings, and its Naples, Vesuvius, and sugar plums stayed in her mind for life. Francisco and Piedro became her daily companions. Her introduction testifies how Edgeworth's stories of children, first published in the 1790s, held young readers a century later.
the-phantom-ship-2:
Captain Frederick Marryat's The Phantom Ship, labeled part 2 in this record, opens with Chapter One in mid-seventeenth-century Holland. Near Terneuse, on the Scheldt opposite Walcheren, stands a small cottage once painted deep orange with vivid green shutters and blue and white tiles. Its colors have faded, tiles have fallen, and one front room has been sealed for nearly seventeen years, seen by no eye.

Inside the neat kitchen sit a worn, beautiful widow of about forty, with flashes of madness in her eyes, and her son Philip, a stout, daring youth of nineteen or twenty. She begs him not to go to sea, though staying means starving. He asks whether his father drowned at sea, and she falls to prayer. A family curse stirs.
the-philippines-past-and-present-volume-: Dean C. Worcester, Secretary of the Interior of the Philippine Islands from 1901 to 1913, wrote The Philippines Past and Present, in two volumes with 128 plates. Volume I is dated 1914. A frontispiece caption shows Emilio Aguinaldo beside a corn field as a sign of peace under American rule. That caption, the title page, and part of a contents list are present; the chapters themselves are not. The list asks Was Independence Promised? and Did We Destroy a Republic?, then turns to civil government.
the-physiology-of-marriage-part-2:
Second part of Honoré de Balzac's The Physiology of Marriage carries the heading Means of Defence, Interior and Exterior. It opens at Meditation X, a treatise on marital policy, with a motto taken from Hamlet. The husband addressed here now fears that another man may possess his wife. That fear wakes his passion again, through pride, selfishness, or self-interest.

Balzac lays down three principles for the husband's conduct. He should never believe what a woman says. He should look for the spirit behind her actions rather than the letter. He should remember that a woman is never more busy than when she keeps quiet. Skill, readers are told, lies less in knowing such rules than in applying them. The husband must practise constant concealment, like a rider watching the ears of a tricky horse.
the-pillars-of-the-house-or-under-wode-u: Volume I of Charlotte M. Yonge's The Pillars of the House, or Under Wode, Under Rode, was published in London by Macmillan and Co. in 1875. Here only the title page and contents appear, so the novel itself is absent. Chapter titles run from The Birth-Day Gift, The Pic-Nic, and Fortunatus' Purse through Working for Bread and The Choral Festival. Later entries include Giant Despair's Castle, Pegasus in Harness, The Winter of Discontent, Midsummer Sun, and By the River.

Volume II of Charlotte M. Yonge's The Pillars of the House, or Under Wode, Under Rode, was published in London by Macmillan and Co. in 1875. It continues the two-volume novel. Here only the title page and the first contents entries appear, so the story itself is absent. The numbering carries on from the first volume. Chapter XXIV is titled Family Ghools and Chapter XXV Don Giovanni. A sibling record holds the matching front matter and contents of Volume I.
the-poems-of-jonathan-swift-d-d-volume-2: Volume II of The Poems of Jonathan Swift, D.D., was edited by William Ernst Browning and published by G. Bell and Sons at London in 1910, matching Volume I. Here only the title page and contents appear; the poems themselves are absent. The volume opens with Cadenus and Vanessa. To Love, a rebus by Vanessa, and the Dean's answer follow. Entries circle around Stella: birthday poems, verses to and by her, and a receipt to restore her youth. Pieces on Dingley and Brent and on Death and Daphne also appear.
the-poetical-works-of-alexander-pope-vol:
Volume II of The Poetical Works of Alexander Pope was issued in 1856, with memoir, critical dissertation, and notes by the Reverend George Gilfillan. It opens with an essay on the genius and poetry of Pope. Few poets, it begins, drew so much admiration and so much abuse in their own lifetime. Flattery and detraction fell on him together. Argument over his claims has raged ever since.

The essay sorts his enemies by motive. Some could not bear a Papist as the nation's principal bard. Zealous Whigs wanted no Tory translating Homer. Grub Street growled that poets should be poor while Pope stayed independent, and others mocked his grotto. His friendships with Lords Oxford and Bolingbroke, his testy temper, and his small, misshapen body all drew fire. That fire had little to do with the merit of his verse.
the-poetical-works-of-edward-young-volum: Volume II of The Poetical Works of Edward Young was published at Boston by Little, Brown and Company in 1859. Here only the title page and contents appear, so the poems themselves are absent. The contents list The Last Day in three books and The Force of Religion in two. Love of Fame follows in seven satires, the fifth and sixth on women. An Ocean ode, a paraphrase on Job, and a letter to Mr. Tickell on Addison's death also appear. Resignation and two epistles to Pope close the list.
the-pomp-of-the-lavilettes-volume-2:
Volume 2 of Gilbert Parker's The Pomp of the Lavilettes opens in the middle of the novel, at Chapter X, with no front matter at all. Ferrol is recovering from his injuries faster than expected. Christine has made herself his constant nurse. Her mother, Madame Lavilette, means to defy the parish priest. Marriage into the nobility would justify her long-baffled hopes. The parish gossips while the Regimental Surgeon visits late.

Half asleep in an arbour of the Manor garden, Ferrol overhears Nic Lavilette talking with a stranger. The man has raised five thousand dollars, every cent the two counties could yield. It waits at the Seigneury under an order on the Seigneur Duhamel. Nic is to carry it to headquarters in two days, on General Papineau's orders. The voices pass, and Ferrol sits moveless. He thinks how that money would ease his own situation.
the-portrait-of-a-lady-volume-2:
Volume II of Henry James's The Portrait of a Lady opens in mid-story at Chapter XXVIII. The next evening finds Lord Warburton calling again on his friends at their hotel. He learns they have gone to the opera. He drives after them and gains admittance to one of the secondary theatres. There he scans the tiers of boxes in the large, bare, ill-lighted house until he finds the party.

Miss Archer, Isabel, sits facing the stage, partly screened by the curtain of the box. Mr. Gilbert Osmond leans back beside her. Warburton watches the pair and asks himself whether he should interrupt their harmony. On the staircase he meets Ralph Touchett descending slowly, hat tipped at the inclination of ennui. Ralph complains that his cousin has a visitor. Miss Stackpole and Bantling have gone out for an ice, and the opera is very bad.
the-prince-and-the-pauper-part-2:
Part 2 of Mark Twain's The Prince and the Pauper opens at Chapter V, Tom as a Patrician. The part files divide the novel into slices, and this one begins with Tom Canty alone in the prince's cabinet. Tom makes good use of his chance. He turns before the great mirror admiring his finery and imitates the prince's high-bred carriage. He draws the beautiful sword and bows with it, kisses the jewelled dagger, and tries the sumptuous chairs.

He wonders how proud the Offal Court herd would think him, could they peep in at his grandeur. After half an hour he notices the prince has been gone long. Loneliness turns to fear: someone may catch him in the prince's clothes with no prince to explain. They might hang him first and inquire afterward. A page then announces the Lady Jane Grey, and a richly clad young girl bounds toward him.
the-purcell-papers-volume-2:
Volume two of Joseph Sheridan Le Fanu's posthumous tales carries the same Graves memoir heading as its companion volume and turns at once to fiction. Its first piece is framed as a fifth extract from the papers of the late Francis Purcell, parish priest of Drumcoolagh.

That opening narrative comes in a woman's hand and concerns a countess whose two great families have both died out. Around it sit a bridal tale, an account of Schalken the painter, and scraps of Irish ballads. The framing device lets private, painful family history be told while names that might cause harm are altered or withheld.
the-seaboard-parish-volume-2:
Volume two of George MacDonald's The Seaboard Parish opens with another Sunday evening. Its contents add Niceboots, a blacksmith, and a life-boat. Mr. Percivale, the shadow of death, and a walk to church appear. The list closes with a small adventure and the harvest.

In the opening chapter, the family meets in Connie's room for their talk. The window stands open and the sun is in the west. Below, the sea lies bluer than a listener could believe, Dora reports seeing Niceboots at church. He stared at her father as if he had never heard a sermon before, she says. Connie answers with perfect confidence. She had not heard the sermon herself, the narrator notes dryly.
the-seats-of-the-mighty-volume-2:
Volume two of Gilbert Parker's The Seats of the Mighty holds chapters seven to thirteen of Captain Robert Moray's memoirs. Its headings include As Vain as Absalom and The Coming of Doltaire. A little boast closes the volume's list.

Chapter seven, Quoth Little Garaine, finds Moray long imprisoned. He explains that his story was not written in one Sunday afternoon. Its making took many weeks. In all that time he saw no face but Gabord's. Gabord brought bread and water twice a day. He would answer no questions about Juste Duvarney, Voban, or Doltaire. Moray had no light, yet he trained himself to see in the dark. After a month he could make out his dungeon's outlines. A mouse, lured by scattered crumbs, became his companion.
the-settlers-in-canada-2: Captain Marryat's Settlers in Canada appears in this second record with a Routledge title page. George Routledge and Sons sold it in London and New York. A transcriber's note says the table of contents was added by the transcriber. That contents gives only chapter numbers, running past thirty-two, with no titles. The pages shown here stop at the title matter and that numbered list, so no story text appears.
the-shaving-of-shagpat-an-arabian-entert: Volume two of George Meredith's The Shaving of Shagpat is represented here solely by a Project Gutenberg header. That header numbers the e-text 4402 and dates its release to September 2003. It was first posted on December 21, 2001, the header adds. Pat Castevans and David Widger are named as its producers. Standard project notices fill the remaining pages shown. They concern copyright laws, file keeping, and donations. Meredith's text, title page, and contents are all absent. Nothing of the entertainment's second volume can be reported from this record.
the-sisters-volume-2:
Volume two of Georg Ebers's The Sisters opens at chapter seven, inside Memphis. The old palace of the kings stood amid the white wall's bastions and ramparts, Ebers writes. The stately brick structure had courts, corridors, chambers, and halls without number. Gayly painted wooden out-buildings surrounded it. A magnificent pillared banqueting hall stood in the Greek style.

Verdant gardens ringed the palace, tended by a host of laborers. They kept the tanks clean and fed the fish in them. A beast-garden held animals from the heavy-treading elephant to the light-footed antelope. Loud barkings came from the dog-kennels, and neighing from the stables. Cleopatra's apartments sat high in the building, the passage explains. In summer she preferred airy tents on the palace roof, guarded day and night. No translator is named in the pages shown for this volume.
the-spectator-volume-2:
Volume two of Henry Morley's three-volume edition of The Spectator came from George Routledge and Sons in London in 1891. It reproduces the eighteenth-century periodical essays as first issued and as corrected by their authors. The text present here opens at number 203, dated Tuesday, October 23, 1711, and signed by Addison.

That essay turns on a loose tribe of men the writer says he has not yet taken notice of, who ramble into every corner of London to seduce unfortunate women. These profligates, he charges, raise children in every quarter of town. They often father them upon the church-warden for a consideration. Married men are left with small families in most parishes, and bachelors are similarly encumbered.
the-star-chamber-an-historical-romance-v: Volume two of W. Harrison Ainsworth's historical romance, issued with the first by Bernhard Tauchnitz at Leipzig in 1854, continues the Star-Chamber story. Only the title page and contents are present here. The contents list twenty-six chapters. They cover poison and counter-poison, and the forged confession produced. A wager between the Conde de Gondomar and the Marquis of Buckingham follows. Sir Jocelyn's disgrace and arrest come next. The old Fleet Prison and an abduction close the list. The narrative itself does not appear.
the-talk-of-the-town-volume-1-of-2: James Payn's Talk of the Town came out in two volumes from Smith, Elder in London, and this record shows the second edition of 1885. Only the title page of volume one is present. A frontispiece caption shows Miss Margaret looking up from her plate, smiling a welcome. No chapters follow in what is shown. Readers can place the book, its publisher, and its year, and glimpse one character's name, but Payn's story itself never begins here.
the-talk-of-the-town-volume-2-of-2: Volume two of James Payn's Talk of the Town, in Smith, Elder's second edition of 1885, continues the two-volume novel begun in the first record of the pair. The pages present here give a frontispiece line, the title page, and the first contents entry, chapter nineteen, called Another Discovery. Nothing of Payn's actual chapters is shown. A shouted frontispiece caption, 'Begone! both of you,' hints at a quarrel waiting inside, yet the quarrel itself and everything around it remain outside this record.
the-three-cities-trilogy-lourdes-volume-:
Volume two of Zola's Lourdes, in Ernest A. Vizetelly's translation, opens on the second day at twenty minutes past three by the Lourdes station clock. Shadowy figures pace the platform, resignedly waiting for the white train. Among them walks Father Fourcade, director of the national pilgrimage, a sixty-year-old who looks like a general inflamed to conquer. Gout makes him drag one leg, so he leans on Dr. Bonamy of the Miracle Verification Office.

Fourcade questions the station-master, who reports the white train only ten minutes late while fretting over the Bayonne train. Zola sets the machinery of organized pilgrimage in motion: officials, doctors, and verifiers of miracles all waiting on a timetable. The sick are coming, and the great question of what counts as a cure hangs over the platform.
the-three-cities-trilogy-paris-volume-2:
Book Two of Zola's Paris, in Ernest A. Vizetelly's translation, brings Pierre home to his little house at Neuilly with his wounded brother Guillaume. The cab ride from the scene of the outrage passed in terrible silence, Guillaume sinking down and saying nothing. Pierre feared he would faint and wondered which surgeon could be trusted with the secret. At the Arc de Triomphe Guillaume finally spoke: no doctor; they would attend to the wound together.

Pierre waved away the prohibition, ready to disobey if needed, and helped his brother up the steps unseen by any neighbour. Zola binds the priest to his revolutionary brother's hidden life. The quiet, shuttered house and dark garden hold a family secret that could destroy them both, and Pierre has just sworn himself to keeping it.
the-three-cities-trilogy-rome-volume-2:
Part Two of Zola's Rome, in Ernest A. Vizetelly's translation, opens with Pierre planning his first Roman visit. After publishing 'New Rome,' he received a flaming protest from old Count Orlando Prada, hero of Italian independence, who accused him of forgetting Italy. Their correspondence grew warm, and Pierre promised to call. Yet his lodging at the Boccanera mansion complicates things, since Benedetta fled the count's son and seeks an annulment.

Pierre confides in Benedetta, who urges him to go at once, calling Orlando a national glory whom all Italy names with affection. She grew up among people who likened him to Satan, then learned to love him. Zola sets the priest between old Italy's feuding houses, where a courtesy call is a political act.
the-tragic-comedians-a-study-in-a-well-k:
Volume two of George Meredith's Tragic Comedians, dated 1892, opens at Book Two, chapter seven, with Alvan hurrying down to the plains to Clotilde. Meeting him is like summer morning sunlight striking through her blood, dissolving the strangeness that gathers during absences. She has grown reconciled to his startling messages, yet she means to speak practically about measures leading to their union. One subject her parents will raise is the baroness, and she asks to see a photograph.

Alvan produces one and watches her eyelids, those revealers of the critical mind, droop nearly shut in deadly criticism. The budless grey woman disenchanted her; Alvan, colouring, names a grandmaternal birth year and protests she was fair twenty years back. Meredith anatomizes courtship by photograph, a whole engagement wobbling over one square card.
the-trail-of-the-sword-volume-2:
Volume two of Gilbert Parker's Trail of the Sword opens Epoch Two in a low stone house on Notre Dame Street, Montreal. Parker paints winter Montreal and Quebec as cheerful as any city under a cordial sky, where men loved, hated, and bargained, doing brave deeds lightly. Through a window one might see a priest joyously playing a violin, an instrument many then called devilish. The room holds a crucifix, a gun, snow-shoes, and a sword.

The priest is Dollier de Casson, so tall and powerful that, rising in musical exaltation, his head almost touches the ceiling, the violin a toy under his chin. Parker warms his tale of Iberville's wars with this portrait of a fighting, fiddling churchman. Friends in council, as the chapter is called, set plots moving while music plays.
the-translation-of-a-savage-volume-2:
Volume two of Gilbert Parker's Translation of a Savage opens with chapter six, The Passing of the Years, after Lali's accident and slow recovery. A change has come on her: the last desire for savage life went with that strange ride. She understands now that her husband never loved her and married her as an instrument of retaliation. She forbids the family to write him news of her, beyond saying she is well, and later forbids word of her child's birth.

The fair-haired child grows like his father, and the Armours name him Richard, after Lali's best friend among them and by her wish. Motherhood gives Lali new purpose and a schooled pride. One wrinkle: this record's contents also list chapter nine here, though the complete edition places it in volume three, a small clash between the two listings.
the-travels-of-marco-polo-volume-2: Volume two of Marco Polo's Travels in the Yule-Cordier edition contains the second volume of the 1903 edition plus Cordier's 1920 volume of addenda, two original volumes bound as one. The pages present here give its title and a synopsis of contents, opening with Book Two continued and a journey to the west and south-west of Cathay. Appendices and an index are also promised. Polo's marvels do not appear in what is shown, so this record documents the great edition's architecture, not its storytelling.
the-trespasser-volume-2:
Volume two of Gilbert Parker's Trespasser opens with chapter six, Strange Encounters, a few hours after the last events. Gaston sits his horse in a secluded spot while his uncle sketches him. Saracen will not stay quiet, and the sketch astonishes Gaston with its force. He rides through park and village to the moor and looks down on a perfect landscape without villa, cottage, or factory chimney. Village noises soothe him, and the woodland smell drifts over.

There the question lands: was his uncle right that he is out of place here? Gaston has learned fine social ways and a distinguished native courtesy taught by his father where no social functions used it. Yet he does things his family's friends could not and would not do. Parker studies a colonial-born heir suspended between wilderness candour and English artifice.
the-wits-and-beaux-of-society-volume-2:
Volume two of The Wits and Beaux of Society, by Grace and Philip Wharton, appeared in 1890. Justin Huntly McCarthy edited this edition. Illustrations by H. K. Browne and James Godwin are retained. The contents open with a long life of Horace Walpole. His childhood in Arlington Street begins the account.

Walpole's schooldays and friendship with the poet Gray follow. His father Sir Robert's fall from office is covered. So are the great house at Houghton and its picture gallery. Walpole's later years at Strawberry Hill close the section. Readers interested in eighteenth-century society will find rich anecdote here.
the-works-of-guy-de-maupassant-volume-2: Volume two of The Works of Guy de Maupassant, subtitled Monsieur Parent and Other Stories, appears here as a contents list only. Seventeen stories are named in the list. They include A Vagabond, Useless Beauty, and That Pig of a Morin. A Normandy Joke and The Sequel to a Divorce also appear. The volume carries a 1909 copyright by Bigelow, Smith and Company. The stories themselves are absent from the pages present.
the-works-of-lord-byron-letters-and-jour: Volume two of Byron's Letters and Journals, edited by Rowland E. Prothero, appears here as a partial list of letters. The list opens mid-sequence at letter 169, written to publisher John Murray. Letters to R. C. Dallas and Augusta Leigh follow closely. Francis Hodgson and James Wedderburn Webster also receive letters. Dates run through August into October. The letter texts themselves are absent from the pages shown in this record.
the-works-of-the-highly-experienced-and-: The Works of John Rudolph Glauber, second copy, 1689. The chemist's works. This book preserves that collection. The archive keeps the paper open to all. Its pages add to the record of the past. Scholars prize such firsthand sources.
the-world-for-sale-volume-2:
Gilbert Parker's second volume of The World for Sale opens with book two, chapter eight, The Sultan. Ingolby questions Jowett, a horse-dealer, with sharp urgency. Horse theft, he warns, means a penitentiary sentence if proved. Jowett is shrewd, vain, and quick with humor. Both rival towns like him despite his sharp dealing. He has beaten each town in horse trades many times.

His taste for low company is widely gossiped about. Parker sketches a frontier town personality in a few strokes. Ingolby's forceful leadership drives the wider story. Readers get Canadian frontier rivalry, romance, and scheming. The volume continues a tale split across three books.
the-writings-of-samuel-adams-volume-2: An old Project Gutenberg header is all that this record shows for volume two of The Writings of Samuel Adams. Harry Alonso Cushing collected and edited the writings. The header dates the electronic text to March 2000. This volume covers Adams's writings from 1770 to 1773. Adams's letters and essays themselves do not appear within the pages present here, beyond the header's title and editor information.
their-silver-wedding-journey-volume-2:
Part II of William Dean Howells's travel novel begins at chapter XXVI, with the Marches arriving in Carlsbad. Burnamy meets them at the station, and Mrs. March scolds him warmly for the trouble. She also notices what he leaves unsaid about Leipsic and his employer.

The drive into town gives Howells room for a crowded promenade scene along the Tepl river. Germans, Poles, Austrian officers, Greek priests, Russians, and Americans mingle in bright streets. Readers get close social observation, gentle comedy, and a European spa town rendered through the eyes of American visitors.
theological-essays-and-other-papers-volu:
Volume two of Thomas De Quincey's theological essays and other papers ranges from the secession from the Church of Scotland to Milton, Charlemagne, and modern Greece. One piece considers Lord Carlisle on Pope, and another describes the toilette of a Hebrew lady. The secession essay dates from 1844.

De Quincey warns English readers that Scotland's church crisis confuses them because church and court language differ across the border. He promises to lead the discussion through four main questions. Readers get a second miscellany where theology, biography, and classical subjects sit side by side.
theologico-political-treatise-part-2: Part two of Baruch Spinoza's Theologico-Political Treatise covers chapters six to ten, presented through a detailed contents list. Chapter six treats miracles and denies that breaking natural law makes sense. Chapter seven argues scripture should be interpreted by scripture itself. Chapter eight concludes the Pentateuch was not written by Moses, and separates his actual writings. Rival methods, including Maimonides and the traditions of Pharisees and Papists, are marked for rejection. Only the contents summaries are held in this record, so the chapters themselves are not shown.
theophrastus-bombastus-von-hohenheim-par: A Columbia University microfilm header from 1992 opens this record, part of a preservation project funded by the National Endowment for the Humanities. Its cataloguing card names the author as Edward Schubert. The title begins Theophrastus Bombastus von Hohenheim, with London and 1893 given as place and date. That card points to the same Paracelsus bibliography sold by William Wesley and Son in the sibling record. Here the preservation header and card are what is present, so Schubert's catalogue entries themselves do not appear.
theophrastus-enquiry-plants-hort-vol-2:
Volume two of Hort's Loeb Theophrastus continues the Enquiry into Plants. The 1916 translation completes the ancient world's complete botany. Greek text faces English in the Loeb format throughout the volume.

Trees and timber receive extended treatment for builders and shipwrights. Shrubs, herbs, grains, and vegetables follow with their cultivation lore. Theophrastus records what farmers and woodcutters knew by practice. Medicine draws on many plants he catalogs, and he notes their powers. Aristotle's heir keeps his eyes on the green world in every chapter. The two Hort volumes together give the fullest ancient botany we possess. Gardeners can still read him with recognition and pleasure.
theoria-philosophiae-hermeticae-septem-t: Theoria philosophiae hermeticae, 1617, second copy, the hermetic theory. This book preserves that work. The paper lived through the years. It waits for future eyes. It holds its historical place. It is kept for readers to consult. It is kept for study by scholars.
theurgia-goetia-lemegeton-part-2:
The Theurgia-Goetia is Part Two of the Lemegeton, a famed book of spirit craft. Joseph H. Peterson made this text from Sloane MS 3825, a hand book of the 1600s. The Lemegeton runs to four parts in all, with the Goetia first. This part deals with the spirits of the air.

Seals, names, and ranks of the air chiefs fill the text in full. Calls and bonds tell the mage how to raise and rule each spirit. The spirits are said to be part good and part ill in their bent. The text is a chief source for the rite magic of its age.
thierry-norman-conquest-vol-2:
Volume 2 of Thierry's Norman Conquest history, in Hazlitt's 1847 English, covers William's reign. The Conqueror rules a sullen land while English revolts flare and fail. Thierry keeps his lens fixed on the losers of 1066 throughout.

Castles rise, lands change hands, and the old nobility fades away. Thierry tells the tale as a yoke laid on a whole people. His Romantic fire makes dry records read like a nation's lament. Critics fault his bias, yet none deny his grip on readers. The volume completes his famed, fierce retelling of England's great turning point. Its passion shaped how France and England recalled 1066 for decades.
thirlwall-history-greece-vol-2:
Volume 2 of Thirlwall's History of Greece, from 1845, shows Sparta and Athens rising. Lycurgus the lawgiver and Solon the reformer lead the twin tales. The age of the tyrants fills the space between their reforms.

Athens curbs its nobles while Sparta drills its famed citizen army. Colonies spread Greek life across two seas in these busy years. Thirlwall's calm, fair narrative shows the city-states taking lasting shape. His judgments stay measured even where old sources clash and lie. The forms that would define the West emerge in this volume. Few guides handle the tangled early record with such poise.
tocqueville-democracy-in-america-reeve-v:
The second volume of Alexis de Tocqueville's Democracy in America came out in 1840, five years after the first. Henry Reeve again supplied the English translation. Where volume one studied America's institutions, this one studies its thoughts, feelings, and daily life.

Tocqueville asks how equality reshapes religion, family, ambition, and the love of money. He fears a soft despotism: citizens shrunk into private life while a mild, vast power manages them. He also finds hope in free association, the habit of joining for common ends. Many readers judge this volume the deeper and more prophetic of the two.
travels-in-morocco-volume-2: Volume two of James Richardson's Travels in Morocco, edited by his widow, opens with a full table of contents. Its chapters cover Jewish life at Mogador, the Jews of the Atlas, and disputes between Jews and Moors. Later chapters take up the Moroccan dynasties, the character of Muley Abd Errahman, and dealings with European powers. Only the title page and contents are present here, so the chapters themselves do not appear. The contents also promise geography, soil, and climate.
tuzk-i-jahangiri-rogers-vol-2:
Volume 2 of the Tuzuk-i-Jahangiri appeared in Rogers and Beveridge's version in 1914. Jahangir's memoirs run on through the later years of his reign. The emperor's voice grows wearier as health and power slip away.

Nur Jahan, his gifted queen, rises to real power at court. Princes rebel, campaigns drag, and the emperor's drinking takes its toll. Jahangir still notes art, beasts, and odd events with a sharp eye. Power, pleasure, and death close in across his final chapters here. The twilight of a reign glows in his own unguarded words and notes. Few royal memoirs end on so frank and human a note.
tylor-primitive-culture-1871-vol-2:
The second volume of Tylor's Primitive Culture, from 1871, carries his scheme of religion's growth to its height. Volume one set out survivals and animism; this one traces belief as it climbs. Tylor follows the development of religion from the doctrine of souls upward.

Spirits grow into nature gods, gods gather into ordered pantheons, and polytheism strains toward one supreme deity. Rites, sacrifices, and prayers are tracked through the same ascent. The evolutionary ladder dominated anthropology for fifty years before critics dismantled its rankings. Even so, Tylor's mass of evidence and clear prose keep the volume alive. It completes the masterwork of Victorian anthropology.
un-doc-administrative-instruction-st-ai-: Administrative Instruction ST/AI/189/Add.9/Rev.2 — a UN staff rule on internal procedures. It lays out the inside rules that UN workers must follow. The instruction is the staff rulebook: the inside rules for UN staff, filed here in full session twice.
un-doc-united-nations-human-rights-counc:
Sri Lanka's record after its civil war stands at the center of Human Rights Council resolution 19/2, adopted in Geneva in March 2012. The Council is the main United Nations body for human rights. The United States led the push for the text, which passed by a divided vote.

The resolution welcomes Sri Lanka's own inquiry report but says its advice was not fully carried out. It calls on Colombo to act on accountability for wartime abuses and to accept UN help. The vote marked a shift: the Council now pressed Sri Lanka directly, after years of praise.

Violence and unfair treatment based on sexual orientation and gender identity are the focus of Human Rights Council resolution 32/2, adopted in June 2016. The Council is the chief United Nations body for human rights. The vote was close, and debate around it was fierce.

The resolution creates a new post: an independent expert on this form of violence and bias. The expert is tasked with studying abuses, sharing good practice, and talking with states. Supporters hailed a landmark for gay and trans rights. Critics said the Council had stepped into matters of culture and faith.
un-ga-res-2:
Five tongues would speak for the new United Nations, and Resolution 2, passed on 1 February 1946, sets the rule. The annex names Chinese, French, English, Russian, and Spanish as the official tongues of all UN bodies, save the world court. English and French alone serve as working tongues, the pair in which daily business is done.

Speeches in a working tongue are rendered into the other. Speeches in the other three official tongues are rendered into both. A delegate may also speak in any other tongue, at the cost of providing the rendering. The Assembly urges all other UN bodies to adopt the same rules, and asks for a study of phone-based live translation.
un-ga-res-a-69-2:
Heads of state and chiefs from across the world met at UN headquarters in New York on 22 and 23 September 2014 for the World Conference on Indigenous Peoples. Resolution A/69/2 adopts the outcome text of that meeting. The assembled chiefs pledge fresh fealty to the aims of the Charter, in a spirit of joint work with the native peoples of the world.

The text welcomes the ground work of the native peoples themselves, above all the world meet at Alta, in Norway, in June 2013. It states fresh backing for the UN Declaration on the Rights of Indigenous Peoples. The UN's role in guarding those rights, the chiefs hold, stays both weighty and lasting.
un-ga-res-es-11-2:
War's human toll in Ukraine fills Resolution ES-11/2, passed by the General Assembly in emergency session on 24 March 2022. The text backs Ukraine's freedom, unity, and land in full, out to its waters. Russia's attack inside Ukraine, it says, has brought a scale of suffering Europe has not seen in decades. The Secretary-General's plea that Russia halt its attack is backed in plain terms.

Aid must reach all who need it, the vote holds, and civilians must be shielded from harm. States near Ukraine that took in crowds of the fleeing are praised. The text was the Assembly's second vote of the emergency session, after the call for Russia to pull out. It passed by 140 votes to five.
un-ga-res-united-nations-general-assembl:
General Assembly Resolution 2, adopted on 1 February 1946, set the language rules of the United Nations. The annexed rules made Chinese, French, English, Russian, and Spanish the official languages, with English and French as the working languages used day to day.

Under the rules, speeches in one working language were interpreted into the other, and speeches in the other official languages into both. Word-for-word records were kept in the working languages, short records in all official ones, and all resolutions were issued in the official languages. The Assembly also urged the other organs to adopt like rules, and asked for study of telephone interpretation systems.

General Assembly resolution 69/2 adopts the outcome document of the World Conference on Indigenous Peoples, the Assembly's high-level meeting held in New York on 22 and 23 September 2014. Governments meeting there recommit to the United Nations Declaration on the Rights of Indigenous Peoples, adopted in 2007.

The outcome document commits states to consult and cooperate with indigenous peoples through their own institutions. It commits them to seek free, prior, and informed consent before measures that affect them. It commits them to build national action plans to carry out the Declaration. It promises better data, equal access to education and health care, and protection for indigenous women and children. It promises respect for rights over lands, territories, and resources. It also asks for a system-wide United Nations action plan. The conference turned the Declaration from a statement of rights into a program of national follow-through.

Resolution ES-11/2 of the General Assembly, adopted at the eleventh emergency special session in 2022, deals with the humanitarian consequences of the aggression against Ukraine. It follows resolution ES-11/1 of 2 March 2022. That resolution's demand for the complete withdrawal of Russian forces is repeated here. The text responds to a humanitarian crisis it describes as unseen in Europe for decades.

The Assembly demands an immediate end to the hostilities by the Russian Federation, above all attacks on civilians and civilian objects. It demands that sieges of cities, in particular Mariupol, be lifted. It calls for safe humanitarian access. It calls for protection of medical and aid workers, hospitals and supplies. It calls for respect for international humanitarian law. It asks member states to fund the United Nations humanitarian and refugee response plans in full. The plans are for Ukraine and its neighbours.
un-sc-res-united-nations-security-counci: UN Security Council Resolution 2 — the 1946 resolution urging Iran and the Soviet Union to negotiate over the troop presence. It stands among the Council’s earliest formal acts, from its founding year. The founding-year negotiation is the earliest: the 1946 Soviet-Iran talks urged.
un-un-res-united-nations-human-rights-co: UN Human Rights Council Resolution 32/2 — the Council's 2016 vote numbered 32/2. It put the 2016 stance on record. The 32/2 vote is the 2016 mark: the Council's line that year on file, filed here in full session today.
vedanta-sutras-thibaut-vol-2:
Thibaut's second Vedanta Sutras volume appeared in 1896 with Ramanuja's commentary instead. Ramanuja, the great rival interpreter, read the same sutras very differently. The volume formed part thirty-eight of the Sacred Books of the East.

Ramanuja answers Sankara with a God of love and devotion. Reality stays one, yet holds souls and matter within itself as God's body. Salvation comes through loving surrender rather than knowledge alone. Devotion meets metaphysics on every page of his commentary. Reading both volumes lets students weigh the rivals directly. The debate between these commentators shaped Hindu theology for a thousand years.
visuddhimagga-pe-maung-tin-vol-2:
Part two of Pe Maung Tin's Path of Purity, issued in 1929, continues Buddhaghosa's Visuddhimagga from part one of 1923. The great fifth-century manual of Theravada practice presses on from concentration toward wisdom. The translation was made for the Pali Text Society.

The reader moves through the higher reaches of meditation: the formless attainments, the divine eye and ear, and the recollection of past lives. Then the ground shifts to wisdom, the analysis of mind and matter, and the stages of insight. Buddhaghosa's method is exact and cumulative, step laid on step. With part one, it gives English readers the fullest classic map of Buddhist meditation.
vittoria-volume-2: Volume two of George Meredith's Vittoria stands here behind an old Project Gutenberg header, which names it number 42 in the series of Meredith's works. Nothing beyond that header is present in these pages: no chapter heads, no contents, and no lines of the novel itself. The header speaks of free plain vanilla electronic texts, readable by humans and computers since 1971, and asks for donations to the archive foundation. The tale of Vittoria herself must be sought in the companion records of the set.
voltaire-age-of-louis-xiv-1753-vol-2:
Volume two completes the 1753 English translation of Voltaire's Age of Louis XIV, first published in French in 1751. Voltaire treated the reign of the Sun King as a whole civilization, not a mere line of battles. The two English volumes of 1753 carried that new kind of history to British readers at once.

In this second volume the age unfolds in its courts, churches, arts, and wars, all weighed by one sharp mind. Voltaire praises the glory and notes the cost, especially where pride drove France to ruin. His method, history as the story of a whole society, founded a school. The Age of Louis XIV remains his most durable work of history.
vyse-operations-gizeh-vol-2:
Volume Two of Howard Vyse's Operations continues the 1837 work at Gizeh. The colonel's crews kept digging, hauling, and recording through the season. More tombs, stones, and finds pass through his journal.

Vyse logs labor, costs, and quarrels with the same care as finds. He describes shafts and chambers as his men cleared them. The detail lets later scholars retrace work long since altered. The tone stays brisk and sure. For readers of the first volume, this record deepens the picture of how Egypt's greatest sites were first explored. Sweat and stone fill every dated page.
wacousta-a-tale-of-the-pontiac-conspirac:
Volume two of John Richardson's Wacousta, or The Prophecy, opens on the evening of the sad day that filled the first volume. For the third time since the siege began, the drawbridge of Detroit is lowered. This time no rattling chains give the garrison away. The bridge drops with a care that speaks of deep secrecy. No armed party stands ready within the walls.

Most of the troops, worn out by the day's harassing duties, have gone to their rest. A few guards pace their posts, less to fight off sleep than to watch what goes on by torchlight in the barrack square. There an anxious knot of officers stands close around two figures. The two figures wear clothes with nothing of the bright soldier about them. Richardson slows the scene to a held breath, before a night errand steals out of the fort.
waverley-or-tis-sixty-years-since-volume:
Volume two of Sir Walter Scott's Waverley, in the same Caledonian series as its first volume, opens at chapter thirty-six, titled An Incident. The scene is an autumn afternoon. Dinner then came at two o'clock. By four, Mr. Gilfillan, a stern Covenanter, begins his march. He hopes to reach Stirling, eighteen miles off, by borrowing an hour or two of the night.

Gilfillan marches stoutly at the head of his followers. He eyes his prisoner from time to time, as if he longs to draw him into argument. At last he drops back beside Waverley's horse.
